                   WESTERN DISTRICT OF WASHINGTON                           
8                            AT SEATTLE                                     
9    In re VALVE ANTITRUST         CASE NO. C21-0563-JCC                    
     LITIGATION                                                             
10                                                                           
                                   ORDER                                    
11                                                                           

12                                                                           
13

15      This matter comes before the Court on the parties’ LCR 37(a)(2) submission (Dkt. No. 
16  164). At issue is whether Gabe Newell should be compelled to appear in person for a Rule 
17  30(b)(1) deposition. (See generally id.) For the reasons described below, the Court finds that Mr. 
18  Newell should so appear.                                                 
19      This is an antitrust suit where Plaintiffs assert Defendant leverages its market power to 
20  charge supra-competitive fees. (See generally Dkt. No. 127.) Discovery is ongoing and Plaintiffs 
21  now seek to depose Mr. Newell, the company’s co-founder, president, and largest shareholder. 
22  (See Dkt. No. 165-2 at 2–4) (notice of deposition). They contend Mr. Newell is uniquely 
23  positioned to testify on all aspects of Defendant’s business strategy. (See Dkt. No. 164 at 21–22.) 
24  For this reason, Plaintiffs assert only an in-person deposition would allow them to adequately 
25  assess Mr. Newell’s credibility. (See generally id.)                     
26      Mr. Newell contends that he is at risk of developing a serious illness were he to contract 
1  COVID-19 and, for this reason, has structured his life to minimize exposure to possible COVID-
2  19 transmission. (See generally Dkt. No. 168.) According to Mr. Newell, an in-person 
3  deposition, even with the health measures which Plaintiffs propose,1 is not consistent with those 
4  safeguards. (Id.) As a result, he seeks a remote deposition. (See Dkt. No. 164 at 3–5.) 
5      This Court may order that a deposition be taken by remote means. See Fed. R. Civ. P. 
6  30(b)(4). In general, it will do so when (a) the party seeking a remote deposition has advanced a 
7  legitimate reason and (b) the opposing party fails to establish that a remote deposition would be 
8  unduly prejudicial. See, e.g., Vargas v. Evergreen Prof. Recoveries Inc., 2022 WL 856991, slip 
9  op. at 1 (W.D. Wash. 2022).                                              
10      The Court appreciates COVID-19’s continued public health risks. (See Dkt. No. 168-1.) 
11  But Mr. Newell presents insubstantial evidence to suggest that he is at a particularized risk of 
12  serious illness (over that of the general public). (See generally Dkt. No. 168.) The measures he 
13  normally takes to minimize COVID-19 exposure, (id.), do not impact this determination. For this 
14  reason, the Court finds Mr. Newell has not advanced a legitimate reason for a remote deposition. 
15  Even if he had, the Court finds Plaintiffs would be unduly prejudiced by a remote deposition 
16  given Mr. Newell’s unique knowledge as to Defendant’s business strategies.2  
17      Accordingly, Mr. Newell is ORDERED to attend the deposition in person as noticed. 
18  (See Dkt. No. 165-2.) In hopes of alleviating Mr. Newell’s health concerns, the Court mandates 
19  the following additional health measures: all participants (including questioning counsel) must 
20  wear a tightly fitting certified N95, KF94, or KN95 face mask throughout the deposition. At his 
21  discretion, Mr. Newell may provide those certified masks to participants. But Mr. Newell shall 
22                                                                           
23      1 This includes use of a well-ventilated large conference room, attendance by only 
  essential people, mask usage by all non-speakers, and rapid at-home COVID testing for all 
24  participants both the day before and again the morning of the deposition. (Dkt. No. 165-2 at 2–
  4.)                                                                       
25                                                                           
       2 While other courts conclude that a deponent’s credibility can be comparably assessed 
26  through remote means, see, e.g., Henry v. Tacoma Police Dept., 2023 WL 5530201, slip op. at 3 
  (W.D. Wash. 2023), this Court is not of that opinion.                     
1  remove his mask when responding to questions from Plaintiffs’ counsel.   
2                                                                           
3      DATED this 16th day of November 2023.

                                     John C. Coughenour
